name: MG92B metal-gear micro servo
description: TowerPro MG92B digital micro servo with metal gears, two ball bearings and an alloy middle case: turns about 180° (90° each way) to the angle set by a 50 Hz pulse of about 1–2 ms (1.5 ms = middle). 3.1 kgf·cm stall torque at 5 V (3.5 kgf·cm at 6 V), 0.13 s/60° at 5 V, 1 µs dead band; runs on 5.0–6.6 V. Sold as: Adafruit Micro Servo - MG92B - 3.5 kg-cm (product #2307), a bare TowerPro MG92B with a 25 cm 3-wire lead and female 2.54 mm JR/Futaba connector (brown GND, red V+, orange/yellow signal), with horns and screws.
eli5: A small but strong motor with metal gears that turns its arm to exactly the angle your board asks for and holds it there.

pins.name: GND
pins.description: Ground (brown wire); join it to the microcontroller's GND

pins.name: V+
pins.description: Servo supply 5.0–6.6 V (red wire); use 5–6 V, never 3.3 V. Stall current is not published (plan for about 1 A)

pins.name: PWM
pins.description: Control pulse (orange/yellow wire): 50 Hz, 1–2 ms high. Adafruit says it wants 5 V logic; use a 3.3→5 V buffer if a 3.3 V pulse is ignored

supplierQuery: TowerPro MG92B metal gear micro servo
buildNotes: Wire colours: brown = GND, red = V+ (5.0–6.6 V), orange (yellow on some leads) = PWM signal.

Power it from a 5–6 V supply, never from the 3.3 V pin. Its stall current is not published; a metal-gear servo of this torque can pull around 1 A when stalled, so use a separate supply for anything beyond a light load and join its ground to the board's GND.
Adafruit warns this servo needs 5 V signals. If it ignores a 3.3 V pulse from an ESP32 or Pico, drive PWM through a 3.3 V → 5 V buffer such as a 74AHCT125 powered from 5 V.
It has no mechanical end stops. 1–2 ms may not give the full 180°; Adafruit suggests trying 0.75–2.25 ms, widened in small steps.
Add a 470 µF capacitor across V+ and GND near the servo if the board resets when it moves.

driver.code:
# TowerPro MG92B metal-gear digital micro servo, MicroPython driver.
# Vendor (Adafruit #2307 / TowerPro): 50 Hz (20 ms) frame; 1.5 ms pulse = middle ("0"),
# ~1 ms = full left ("-90"), ~2 ms = full right ("+90"). Dead band 1 us.
# Supply 5.0-6.6 V. Adafruit notes this servo wants 5 V signal levels: a 3.3 V pulse may
# not be recognised, so drive PWM through a 3.3 V -> 5 V buffer (e.g. 74AHCT125) if it ignores you.
# Angles here run 0..180 degrees: 0 = 1 ms (left), 90 = 1.5 ms (middle), 180 = 2 ms (right).
from machine import Pin, PWM

PERIOD_US = 20000  # 50 Hz frame


class MG92B:
    def __init__(self, pin, min_us=1000, max_us=2000, degrees=180):
        # 1-2 ms may not give the full 180 degrees; Adafruit suggests trying 750-2250 us.
        # This servo has no mechanical end stops: widen in small steps only.
        self.min_us = min_us
        self.max_us = max_us
        self.degrees = degrees
        self.pwm = PWM(pin if isinstance(pin, Pin) else Pin(pin), freq=50)
        self.pwm.duty_u16(0)  # no pulse until an angle is set

    def write_us(self, us):
        us = max(self.min_us, min(self.max_us, us))
        self.pwm.duty_u16(int(us * 65535 // PERIOD_US))

    def angle(self, deg):
        deg = max(0, min(self.degrees, deg))
        self.write_us(self.min_us + (self.max_us - self.min_us) * deg / self.degrees)

    def off(self):
        """Stop sending pulses: the servo goes limp and stops drawing holding current."""
        self.pwm.duty_u16(0)

    def deinit(self):
        self.pwm.deinit()

example.code:
import time
from mg92b import MG92B

servo = MG92B({PWM})
servo.angle(60)
time.sleep(1)
servo.angle(120)
while True:
    time.sleep(1)
